passage: At volleyball practice in São Paulo, Coach Ramos watched Priscila set the ball and shook his head. "Left-handers can't be setters. Never works. Go back to the outside." He had coached for twenty years and said it like a fact. Priscila jogged back, cheeks burning. That night she couldn't stop thinking about it. Twenty years was a lot of years. But her friend Jana had shown her videos of a left-handed setter in the national league, and Priscila's own sets had landed well all week. The next day, stomach fluttering, she stayed after practice. "Coach, can I ask something? I found a left-handed setter in the national league. Could I try for two weeks?" Coach Ramos frowned for a long moment. "Two weeks," he said. "Then we see." She walked out feeling both stupid and brave.

qa.q: How long had Coach Ramos coached?
qa.a: He had coached for twenty years.

qa.q: Why did Priscila feel both stupid and brave walking out?
qa.a: Questioning a coach with twenty years' experience felt awkward and embarrassing, but she trusted the evidence enough to ask anyway.

qa.q: What made Priscila's question respectful?
qa.a: She asked privately after practice, brought a real example, and asked for a short trial instead of telling him he was wrong.

qa.q: How might Coach Ramos see Priscila's question?
qa.a: He might feel challenged at first, as his long frown shows, but respect her effort enough to give her two weeks.

grounding: A teenager weighs a sure-sounding coach's claim against evidence and, awkwardly, asks to test it.

passage: In the packed auditorium of the coaching centre, the director, introduced as "a gold medallist and national topper", told three hundred students, "If you sleep much at all, forget about the entrance exam." Pens scratched. Saurabh wrote it down too, then hesitated. Just last week the school's biology teacher had said teenagers need plenty of sleep to remember what they learn. Two sure voices, two different answers. After the talk, Saurabh caught Sonali by the water cooler. "Do you believe the no-sleep thing?" "He's a national topper," she said. "But is being a topper the same as knowing about sleep?" Saurabh asked, and immediately felt silly. Sonali paused. "Hm. Maybe ask Ma'am again?" He crossed out the note, then half rewrote it in pencil, just in case.

qa.q: How was the director introduced?
qa.a: As a gold medallist and national topper.

qa.q: Why did Saurabh feel silly after asking his question?
qa.a: Doubting a national topper in front of Sonali felt awkward, even though he suspected being a topper isn't the same as knowing about sleep.

qa.q: What is a good next step for Saurabh?
qa.a: He could go back to the biology teacher, whose view is the one to check with here, and look at where each claim comes from rather than trusting whoever sounds most impressive.

qa.q: Why might Sonali lean on the director's title at first?
qa.a: A confident speaker with a big title can feel safer to trust than her own doubt, though her pause shows she starts to question it too.

grounding: A teenager weighs a titled speaker's confident claim against a teacher's and awkwardly starts questioning whether titles guarantee truth.

passage:
Dear Sunaina di,
Something awkward happened. Papa forwarded a message to the whole family group saying every house must register on some website by Friday or the electricity will be cut. He sounded completely sure. He even called Chacha to make him do it. I've always thought Papa knows everything about this stuff; he handles all the bills.
But the website address looked strange, and it asked for bank details. I checked the electricity board's real site. Nothing about it, and there was even a warning about fake messages like this one.
I showed Papa at dinner. My voice was shaking. He went quiet, then said, "Hm, let me check," and later deleted the message from the group. He didn't say sorry, but he didn't scold me either.
Is it wrong that I feel proud and embarrassed at the same time?
Nandini

qa.q: What did the website in the message ask for?
qa.a: It asked for bank details.

qa.q: Why does Nandini feel proud and embarrassed at the same time?
qa.a: Nandini was right to check, which feels good, but correcting Papa, who handles all the bills, felt awkward and a little frightening.

qa.q: What made Nandini's approach sensible?
qa.a: Nandini checked the electricity board's real site, found the warning, and showed Papa calmly at dinner instead of arguing in the family group.

qa.q: How might Papa have felt when shown the warning?
qa.a: Papa probably felt embarrassed after telling Chacha to register, which may be why he went quiet and deleted it without saying sorry.

grounding: A teenager checks a sure-sounding parent's forwarded message, finds it fake, and awkwardly corrects him.

passage:
Okay, Kiran, I'll tell you the whole embarrassing thing. I'm Baljeet, and I used to follow this study channel run by a guy who calls himself "Dr. Brain." White coat, fancy office, speaks like he's sure of everything. He said we only use ten percent of our brains, and his course "unlocks the rest."
I believed it. Why not? He's a doctor, right? So in biology class, when Mrs. Rao was talking about the brain, I put up my hand and said it. Like a fact. With confidence.
She smiled, not unkindly, and asked, "Where's that from?" Then she explained that scans show we use nearly all of it, just not all at once. The class laughed. My ears went red.
That evening I searched "Dr. Brain qualifications." Nothing. The white coat was just a coat. I unsubscribed, but I also felt weird, like, who else have I believed just because they sounded sure?

qa.q: What did 'Dr. Brain' say about how much of our brains we use?
qa.a: He said we only use ten percent of our brains.

qa.q: Why did Baljeet trust 'Dr. Brain' so easily?
qa.a: The white coat, fancy office and confident way of speaking, plus calling himself a doctor, made Baljeet feel he must know the truth.

qa.q: What did Baljeet do after the class laughed, and why was it a useful choice?
qa.a: Baljeet searched for 'Dr. Brain qualifications', found nothing, and unsubscribed, which is a way of checking a claim instead of trusting a title.

qa.q: How might Mrs. Rao have seen Baljeet's answer?
qa.a: Mrs. Rao seemed kind rather than mocking, asking where it came from, perhaps hoping Baljeet would learn to check sources.

grounding: It shows a teenager trusting a confident online 'doctor', then awkwardly learning that titles and certainty do not guarantee truth.

passage:
I'm Santosh, Hansa's older brother, and I drive her to chess class on Saturdays. Her coach, Mr. Iyer, is a former state champion. Everyone treats his word like law. Last month he told her, "Always play this opening. It never loses."
Hansa, sixteen, played it in every game. Then she lost three in a row, all the same way. On the drive home she was quiet, then said, "Bhaiya, what if he's wrong?" and immediately, "No, he's a champion. It must be me."
That night I saw her at the dining table with the board, replaying the three games for hours.
Next Saturday, I waited outside the class. When she came out her cheeks were pink. "I showed him the line where it breaks," she said. "He went silent. Then he said, 'Hm. Show me again.'" She looked both proud and like she wanted to hide under the car seat.

qa.q: How many games in a row did Hansa lose with the opening?
qa.a: She lost three in a row, all the same way.

qa.q: What does Hansa saying 'No, he's a champion. It must be me' suggest she felt?
qa.a: It suggests she trusted Mr. Iyer's title so much that she blamed herself first, and felt uneasy about doubting a champion.

qa.q: What did Hansa do that turned the doubt into something useful?
qa.a: She replayed the three games for hours to find where the opening breaks, then showed Mr. Iyer the exact line, giving evidence instead of just an opinion.

qa.q: How does Santosh see his sister after she comes out of class?
qa.a: Santosh sees her pink cheeks and senses she is both proud and embarrassed, which shows how awkward it felt to question someone she respects.

grounding: Told by a brother, it shows a teenager weighing whether to trust a confident champion coach and awkwardly learning a title doesn't guarantee being right.
